Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Students share first; the example slides come after the share-out. Nobody has to share their own roads or what’s in their backpack. Keep the turn-and-talk open: for you, or for people you know. Test the Crenshaw clip on the school network before the talk.

Every student in the room

Every student carries something, in every skin tone and every kind of family. Money, being the only one, adult jobs at home and long commutes are often invisible at an independent school; name them plainly and move on so nobody feels spotted.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Open warm: “Today is about why this toolkit exists. Short version: your life doesn’t come in separate pieces.”

Slide 2 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Introduce Adrian by who he is before anything happens to him. Ask: “What would be on your sticky notes?” Nobody has to answer out loud.

Slide 3 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Being the big brother is a strength he brings everywhere. Ask: “What’s a role you play at home that people at school might not see?”

Slide 4 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Two languages is a skill, and it can come with extra jobs. Both are true.

Slide 5 · Notes

1 MINUTE. His team is where he belongs. The same thing that gives him his people also costs him some time with others.

Slide 6 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Online is where his art finds an audience. It’s also where comparison sneaks in late at night.

Slide 7 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Pull it together: his identity is a strength at home, at school, with friends and online, and some days it adds weight. Ask: “Where does who you are help you most?”

Slide 8 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Trace one stream with your hand into the lake. Ask: “Which stream has the most water in it for people your age right now?”

Slide 9 · Notes

BEFORE THE TALK: test that this clip plays on the school network and the room’s screen. 2 MINUTES. Click the slide to play Kimberlé Crenshaw’s clip right in the deck, then click to her intersection picture. If it won’t play here, open it on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ViDtnfQ9FHc

Slide 10 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Crenshaw coined the word in 1989 to show how Black women could fall through the cracks of laws that looked at race or gender one at a time. Next slide: everyone has their own crossing.

Slide 11 · Notes

1 MINUTE. “You’re never just one thing.” No one has to name their own roads out loud.

Slide 12 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Don’t ask anyone what’s in their backpack. Say: “You can’t tell from the outside, and that’s the point.”

Slide 13 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Turn and talk with the people next to you. Next slide: share out.

Slide 14 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Take a few answers. Then click for some examples that often come up.

Slide 15 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Ask: “Who’s someone in your life who has been through something hard and came out okay?” No need to share out loud.

Slide 16 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Keep it wide on purpose: some students’ steadying thing is a faith, some a grandmother’s cooking, some a team. All count.

Slide 17 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Code-switching is tiring, and it’s also a skill most adults wish they had. Both are true.

Slide 18 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Turn and talk with the people next to you. Next slide: share out.

Slide 19 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Take a few answers. Then click for some quieter ones people don’t always say out loud.

Slide 20 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Name it plainly. Being “the only one” takes energy most people never notice spending.

Slide 21 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Say it plainly and move on; nobody should feel spotted. Money shapes plans, friendships and stress, and it’s often invisible at a school like ours.

Slide 22 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Lots of students carry adult jobs at home. It can be a source of pride and a real load on the same day.

Slide 23 · Notes

1 MINUTE. When someone seems checked out, sometimes they’re just out of hours.

Slide 24 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Let the line sit. This is the whole reason the toolkit exists.

Slide 25 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Agency matters here: nobody has to use any of it. Use what helps, skip what doesn’t.

Slide 26 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Name the real people: “Ms. Garcia, Dr. Wilson, your advisor. Our doors are open.”

Slide 27 · Notes

4 MINUTES. Take a few answers; any connection counts.

Slide 28 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Close warm. Point out where to find the toolkit and that every page lists a person first.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students meet Adrian, whose identity shows up as strength at home, at school, with friends and online, and sometimes as weight. They see that all of it runs into how they’re doing, hear Kimberlé Crenshaw explain intersectionality in her own words, and share what keeps people going and what weighs them down. They leave knowing the toolkit is there to take what helps, and not to carry it alone.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 2-minute clip “What is Intersectionality?” (NAIS). It plays inside the web deck when you click the Watch slide; the PowerPoint slide opens it on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ViDtnfQ9FHc . Test it on the school network and the room’s screen before the talk.
  • The Student Toolkit link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 6 minMeet Adrian: who he is at home, at school, with friends and online, strength first
  2. 7 minIt all runs to the same place; Crenshaw’s clip; her traffic intersection; everyone has a crossing
  3. 8 minTurn and talk: what keeps you going on a hard week? Share out, then three examples
  4. 8 minTurn and talk: what weighs you down? Share out, then four examples
  5. 6 minMental health is where it all meets, take what helps, don’t carry it alone, turn and talk, close

Short on time (15 minutes)

Meet Adrian and the “same Adrian, all day” slide, it all runs to the same place, the Crenshaw clip and intersection, one turn and talk with its share-out, then mental health is where it all meets, don’t carry it alone and the closing slide.

Before you teach
Nobody speaks for a group.

Invite answers about “you, or people you know.” Never ask a student to explain their culture, faith or family to the room.

Strength first, then the struggle.

Adrian’s story leads with who he is. The “keeps you going” turn-and-talk comes before “weighs you down.” Name struggle plainly; never let it map onto one group.

Money is real here.

Say it plainly once and keep going. The “I’m good, I already ate” slide works because it doesn’t point at anyone.

If something heavy comes up.

Thank the student, keep it short in the room, and connect them with a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Everyone carries something.

Show the range on purpose: students of every skin tone, family shape and income carry things others can’t see.

Families draw on different things.

Faith, food, music, elders, a team, a language. Treat each as a real strength, never as a curiosity.

Money shapes friendships.

Trips, dinners out and the right shoes cost money. Students with less often do quiet math nobody sees.

Two worlds is a skill.

Students who switch languages or settings all day are tired and skilled at once. Both are true.

What the research says

The term intersectionality comes from legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, who used it to describe how race and sex together shaped Black women’s experiences in ways neither one alone explains.

Crenshaw, 1989, University of Chicago Legal Forum

Teens aged 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night for health, learning, mood and attention.

American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus statement (Paruthi et al., 2016, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine)

Across many studies, a positive sense of ethnic-racial identity is linked to better well-being and fewer depressive symptoms in young people.

Rivas-Drake et al., 2014, Child Development

Teens who felt connected at school had lower risks of emotional distress, suicidal thoughts and substance use as adults.

Steiner et al., 2019, JAMA Pediatrics
